--- title: "Ornstein Uhlenbeck Spread Backtest" author: "Rohan Jayanti, Yat Wai Heung" format: html: theme: superhero html-math-method: mathjax toc: true number-sections: true code-fold: true fig-width: 8 fig-height: 4.5 toc-depth: 3 execute: echo: true warning: false message: false jupyter: python3 --- In order to show how the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) process can be applied to pairs trading, we first conduct a backtest on a synthetic spread generated directly from an OU process. This allows the performance of the trading strategy to be evaluated in a controlled manner where the true parameters of the underlying process are known. We will then apply the same methodology to real asset-price data. For the real backtest we will first construct a linear spread from two asset price series and then fit an OU model to the observed spread. ## Backtest on Synthetic Spread We begin by generating a single OU sample path and treating it as if it were an observed spread. Take $$ \theta = 2,\qquad \mu = 0,\qquad \sigma = 1. $$ ::: {#56de0266 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import plotly.graph_objects as go import plotly.io import ornstein_uhlenbeck.ou as ou import ornstein_uhlenbeck.strategy as strategy import ornstein_uhlenbeck.utils as utils from ornstein_uhlenbeck.estimation import estimate_parameters ``` ::: We first simulate a single OU path using the parameters above. ::: {#f109178c .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} params = ou.OUParams( theta = 2.0, mu = 0.0, sigma = 1.0 ) x0 = 0.0 dt = 0.01 n_steps = 20000 n_paths = 1 rng = np.random.default_rng(50) t = ou.time_grid(dt, n_steps) path = ou.simulate_paths(x0, params, dt, n_steps, n_paths, rng) fig = go.Figure() fig.add_trace( go.Scatter( x = t, y = path[:,0], name = "Simulated path", mode = "lines", ) ) fig.add_hline( y = params.mu, line_dash = "dash", annotation_text = "Actual Long-run Mean", ) fig.update_layout( title = "Single Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Sample Path", xaxis_title = "Time", yaxis_title = "State" ) utils.apply_theme(fig) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: We will now devise a trading rule. We will use a standard threshold strategy based on deviations from the long-run mean. In the stationary regime, the OU process has distribution $$ S_t\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{2\theta}\right). $$ Thus the stationary standard deviation is $$ \sigma_S=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{2\theta}}. $$ For the simulated process, the simulated distribution is determined by the true parameters. In the backtest, however, the trading strategy does not have access to these parameters. It therefore uses their estimates obtained exclusively from the training period. We define the trading thresholds as two estimated stationary standard deviations from the estimated long-run mean: - Long spread if $S_t\lt\hat{\mu}-2\hat{\sigma}_S$ - Short spread if $S_t\gt\hat{\mu}+2\hat{\sigma}_S$ - Exit the position when $S_t$ returns to $\hat{\mu}$ We also define the estimated stationary standard deviation: $$ \hat{\sigma}_S = \frac{\hat{\sigma}}{\sqrt{2\hat{\theta}}}. $$ This is a mean-reversion strategy: a sufficiently negative deviation from the estimated mean is taken as an opportunity to take a long position, while a sufficiently positive deviation is interpreted as an opportunity to take a short position. ### Training and Test Data To avoid look-ahead bias, the synthetic path is divided into a training period and a test period. The first 75% of observations are used to estimate the OU parameters. These estimates are then treated as fixed when generating trading signals on the remaining 25% of the path. The final observation of the training period is also included as the first observation of the test period. This provides the starting spread value from which the first test-period position can be evaluated, without using any future test-period observations when estimating the parameters. ::: {#ad38d90d .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} split_index = int(0.75 * len(path)) train = path[:split_index] test = path[split_index - 1:] t_train = t[:split_index] t_test = t[split_index - 1:] estimated_params = estimate_parameters(train, t_train) print(f"True parameters: {params}") print(f"Estimated parameters: {estimated_params}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` True parameters: OUParams(theta=2.0, mu=0.0, sigma=1.0) Estimated parameters: OUParams(theta=np.float64(1.836344043212383), mu=np.float64(-0.02903672365096075), sigma=np.float64(0.9908611398765224)) ``` ::: ::: The parameter estimates can be compared with the known parameters used to generate the synthetic process. | Parameter | True value | Estimated value | |:---|---:|---:| | $\theta$ | 2.00 | 1.8363 | | $\mu$ | 0.00 | -0.0290 | | $\sigma$ | 1.00 | 0.9909 | The estimated parameters can then be used to determine the estimated stationary standard deviation and the corresponding entry thresholds for the out-of-sample test period. ::: {#8e4e8c4f .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} stationary_std = ou.stationary_std(estimated_params) upper_threshold = strategy.upper_threshold(estimated_params) lower_threshold = strategy.lower_threshold(estimated_params) print(f"Estimated stationary standard deviation: {stationary_std:.4f}") print(f"Lower threshold: {lower_threshold:.4f}") print(f"Upper threshold: {upper_threshold:.4f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimated stationary standard deviation: 0.5170 Lower threshold: -1.0631 Upper threshold: 1.0050 ``` ::: ::: We then generate the trading positions from the test-period spread using the estimated parameters. The position takes values in $\{-1,0,1\}$, corresponding to a short position, no position, and a long position respectively. ::: {#de3260ce .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} positions = strategy.gen_positions(test, estimated_params) pnl = strategy.gen_pnl(test, estimated_params) cumulative_pnl = strategy.gen_cum_pnl(test, estimated_params) final_pnl = strategy.gen_final_pnl(test, estimated_params) print(f"Final PnL: {final_pnl:.2f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Final PnL: 12.50 ``` ::: ::: The PnL is calculated from the position held during each interval and the subsequent change in the spread: $$ \mathrm{PnL}_i = P_i(S_{i+1}-S_{i}). $$ Consequently, the position determined from observation $i$ is used to capture the movement from $i$ to $i+1$. This avoids using the future value $S_{i+1}$ when determining the position at time $i$ and therefore avoids look-ahead bias. ### Trade-Level Evaluation For the purpose of trade-level statistics, we define a trade as one complete entry-to-exit cycle. A trade therefore begins when a zero position becomes non-zero and ends when that position subsequently returns to zero. ::: {#b4e1d653 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} number_of_trades = strategy.num_trades(test, estimated_params) average_trade_pnl = strategy.avg_trade_pnl(test, estimated_params) win_rate = strategy.winrate(test, estimated_params) print(f"Number of trades: {number_of_trades}") print(f"Average PnL per trade: {average_trade_pnl:.4f}") print(f"Win rate: {win_rate:.2%}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Number of trades: 11 Average PnL per trade: 1.1364 Win rate: 100.00% ``` ::: ::: The win rate is calculated using completed trades only. This means that a trade which remains open at the end of the test period is not counted when calculating the win rate or the number of completed trades. However, this distinction does not apply to the overall PnL calculation. If a position remains open at the end of the test period, the PnL generated while that position was held is still included in the overall PnL. In other words, the backtest does not artificially close an incomplete final trade merely to classify it as a completed trade at the end of the test period. This means that the final PnL represents the mark-to-market PnL of the strategy over the entire test period. ### Risk and Performance Evaluation The Sharpe ratio is calculated from the full PnL series rather than from individual completed trade PnLs. This is important because the PnL series contains the PnL generated at each time step, including periods where the strategy is not holding a position. For the synthetic backtest we take the risk-free rate to be zero. We therefore use the following PnL-based Sharpe ratio: $$ \mathrm{Sharpe}_{\mathrm{PnL}} = \frac{\overline{\mathrm{PnL}}} {s_{\mathrm{PnL}}}. $$ ::: {#d8eb6d4a .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} sharpe_ratio = strategy.sharpe_ratio(test, estimated_params) print(f"Sharpe ratio: {sharpe_ratio:.4f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Sharpe ratio: 0.0582 ``` ::: ::: We also examine the cumulative PnL and drawdown of the strategy. Cumulative PnL is obtained by summing the incremental PnL through time: $$ C_t = \sum_{i=1}^{t}\mathrm{PnL}_i. $$ Drawdown measures the distance of the cumulative PnL below its historical maximum: $$ D_t = C_t - \max_{s\leq t} C_s. $$ The maximum drawdown is the minimum value of this series. ::: {#5185ec84 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} drawdown = strategy.drawdown(test, estimated_params) max_drawdown = strategy.max_drawdown(test, estimated_params) print(f"Maximum drawdown: {max_drawdown:.4f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Maximum drawdown: -1.0457 ``` ::: ::: We plot the cumulative PnL to show how the strategy's performance develops through the test period. ::: {#274593d9 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig = go.Figure() fig.add_trace( go.Scatter( x = t_test[1:], y = cumulative_pnl, name = "Synthetic PnL accumulation", mode = "lines", ) ) fig.update_layout( title = "Synthetic PnL Accumulation", xaxis_title = "Time", yaxis_title = "Cumulative PnL" ) utils.apply_theme(fig) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The drawdown series provides a complementary view of the strategy's risk by showing the extent to which cumulative PnL falls below its previous high-water mark. ::: {#f7ac2b4f .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig = go.Figure() fig.add_trace( go.Scatter( x = t_test[1:], y = drawdown, name = "Synthetic Drawdown", mode = "lines", ) ) fig.update_layout( title = "Synthetic Strategy Drawdown", xaxis_title = "Time", yaxis_title = "Drawdown" ) utils.apply_theme(fig) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Backtest on Real Spread The real backtest initially presents us with two seperate estimation problems: 1. Estimate the relationship between two assets and construct a spread. 2. Determine whether the spread is well modelled by an OU process and estimate its parameters. ### Starting with Two Asset-Price Series We have obtained data from two correlated oil stocks, SHEL and BP. Let $$ P_t^{\mathrm{SHEL}} = P_t^{(1)} = \mathrm{SHEL price at time} t, $$ and $$ P_t^{\mathrm{BP}} = P_t^{(2)} = \mathrm{BP price at time} t. $$ We wish to exploit the fact that the two companies operate in the same broad industry and therefore have economically related prices. We require a linear combination of the two prices that exhibits mean-reverting behaviour. ### Constructing a Linear Relationship Using OLS We propose the linear model $$ P_t^{1} = \alpha + \beta P_t^{2} + \varepsilon_t. $$ Here: - $\alpha$ is the intercept - $\beta$ is the hedge ratio - $\varepsilon_t$ is the residual. The motivation is that the two prices may have a persistent linear relationship. If BP increases by $\beta$ units of price, we expect SHEL to increase by approximately the corresponding amount, after accounting for the intercept. ### The Hedge Ratio Suppose $$ P_t^{(1)} \approx \alpha + \beta P_t^{(2)}. $$ Then the quantity $$ P_t^{(1)} - \beta P_t^{(2)} $$ should be relatively stable compared with either individual price. This gives us a way of taking a relative-value position rather than betting on whether oil stocks rise or fall. For example, if we are to long the spread, $$ S_t = P_t^{(1)} - \beta P_t^{(2)}, $$ we are to - long one unit of SHEL; - short $\beta$ units of BP. If both stocks rise or fall together, the common movement should cancel. Thus the position is intended to isolate the relative mispricing between the two assets. ### Constructing the Spread Using the fitted regression, define the residual spread as $$ S_t = P_t^{(1)} - \hat{\alpha} - \hat{\beta} P_t^{(2)}. $$ This is equal to the regression residual. ### Fitting the OU Model to the Spread We then hypothesise that the spread $S_t$ follows the OU SDE $$ dS_t = \theta(\mu - S_t)\,dt + \sigma\,dW_t, $$ where the parameters have the usual interpretations. We then estimate the OU parameters and construct our positions in an identical manner to the synthetic backtest. ### Translating the Spread Position into the Two Assets After determining the positions, we trade. Our spread is $$ S_t = P_t^{(1)} - \hat{\alpha} - \hat{\beta} P_t^{(2)}. $$ The constant $\alpha$ does not affect changes in the spread thus $$ \Delta S_t = \Delta P_t^{(1)} - \hat{\beta}\Delta P_t^{(2)}. $$ Hence, a long spread will correspond to - $+1$ SHEL - $-\hat{\beta}$ BP. A short spread will correspond to - $-1$ SHEL - $+\hat{\beta}$ BP. ### Performance Calculation - Incremental PnL - Cumulative PnL - Final PnL - Completed trades - Win rate - Sharpe - Drawdown - Maximum Drawdown ::: {#f7e3c77c .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} # import yfinance as yf # import ornstein_uhlenbeck.strategy as strategy # # prices = yf.download( # ["SHEL", "BP"], # period="5y", # auto_adjust=True, # )["Close"] # # shel = prices["SHEL"].dropna().to_numpy() # bp = prices["BP"].dropna().to_numpy() # # t = [i for i in range(len(bp))] # # alpha, beta = strategy.estimate_hedge_parameters(shel,bp) # # spread = shel - alpha - beta * bp # # fig = go.Figure() # fig.add_trace( # go.Scatter( # x=t, # y=bp, # mode="lines", # name="BP", # ) # ) # # fig.add_trace( # go.Scatter( # x=t, # y=shel, # mode="lines", # name="SHEL", # ) # ) # # fig.update_layout( # title="Stock Prices", # xaxis_title="Trading Days from 24 Aug 2021", # yaxis_title="Prices", # ) # # utils.apply_theme(fig) # fig.show() # # fig = go.Figure() # fig.add_trace( # go.Scatter( # x=t, # y=spread, # mode="lines", # name="Spread", # ) # ) # # fig.update_layout( # title="Spread", # xaxis_title="Trading Days from 21 Aug 2021", # yaxis_title="Spread", # ) # # utils.apply_theme(fig) # fig.show() # # print(f"beta: {beta:.2f}") ``` ::: ::: {#cae0ce72 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} # pnl, positions = strategy.pnl(spread, t) # final_pnl = strategy.final_pnl(pnl) # trade_pnls = strategy.trade_pnls(pnl, positions) # # number_of_trades = strategy.number_of_trades(trade_pnls) # average_trade_pnl = strategy.average_trade_pnl(trade_pnls) # win_rate = strategy.win_rate(trade_pnls, number_of_trades) # sharpe = strategy.sharpe(trade_pnls, average_trade_pnl) # # print(f"Number of trades: {number_of_trades}") # print(f"Average PnL per trade: {average_trade_pnl:.2f}") # print(f"Final PnL: {final_pnl:.2f}") # print(f"Win rate: {win_rate:.2%}") # print(f"Sharpe ratio: {sharpe:.2f}") ``` :::
